'''Steve Granick''' is an American scientist and educator. In 2023 he joined the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|University of Massachusetts-Amherst]] as the Robert Barrett Endowed Chair of Polymer Science and Engineering, with joint appointment in the Chemistry, Physics, and Chemical Engineering Departments<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Department of Polymer Science and Engineering |url=https://www.pse.umass.edu/news/professor-steve-granick-robert-barrett-chair-polymer-science-and-engineering |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=www.pse.umass.edu}}</ref> after serving as director of the [[Institute for Basic Science]] Center for Soft and Living Matter, an interdisciplinary blue-sky research center in [[Ulsan]], [[South Korea]] that pursues [[Basic Science|basic science]] research.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Center for Soft and Living Matter |url=http://softmatt.ibs.re.kr/html/main/main.php |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=softmatt.ibs.re.kr}}</ref> Until 2015 he was professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He is a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]].

== Education ==
Granick obtained his B.A. in [[sociology]] from [[Princeton University]] in 1978 by correspondence and after initially dropping out during his Junior year.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Ravindran|first=Sandeep|date=22 January 2018|title=Profile of Steve Granick|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=115|issue=7|pages=1400&ndash;1402|pmc=5816224|doi=10.1073/pnas.1800048115|pmid=29358386|bibcode=2018PNAS..115.1400R |doi-access=free}}</ref>  He earned his Ph.D. in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of Wisconsin]] in 1982 with [[John D. Ferry]].<ref name=":0" /><!-- PNAS source does not include year of matriculation. -->  He did postdoctoral work at the [[University of Minnesota]] with M. V. Tirrell and at the [[Collège de France]] with Nobel-laureate [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]].<ref name=":0" />

== Academic career ==
Granick joined the faculty of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1985 and rose through the ranks to become Racheff Chair Professor of Materials Science and Engineering and concurrently professor of physics and biophysics, professor of chemistry, and professor of chemical and biomolecular engineering.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Welcome to Granick Group Homepage |url=http://groups.mrl.uiuc.edu/granick/ |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=groups.mrl.uiuc.edu}}</ref>  In 2014, after thirty years at the University of Illinois, he moved to South Korea to join the [[Institute for Basic Science]] (IBS), founding the Center for Soft and Living Matter<ref name=":2" /> with additional appointments as professor of chemistry and physics at [[UNIST]]. In 2023 he joined the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst|University of Massachusetts-Amherst]] as the Robert Barrett Endowed Chair of Polymer Science and Engineering, with joint appointment in the chemistry, physics, and chemical engineering departments.<ref name=":1" />

== Research and achievements ==
Granick is the author of more than 300 scientific articles and has made fundamental contributions to the chemistry and physics of [[soft materials]]. By early 2023, his publications had received over 30,000 citations with h-index of 93.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Steve Granick |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=iCi0XVUAAAAJ&hl=en |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

His research interests range from the study of [[active matter]] to the chemistry and physics of visualized [[macromolecules]], [[Vesicle (biology and chemistry)|vesicles]], and supracolloidal materials. The early work in Granick's career focused on confined liquids. Granick was a pioneer in the field of nanorheology and molecular [[tribology]]. Other early work concerned molecular mobility at polymer surfaces. This progressed to later studies showing how [[biological membrane]]s interact with their environments.<ref name=":0" />

More recently, Granick and his research team work across disciplines to explore imaging, assembly, behavior and interactions of molecules, colloidal particles, and their assemblies. He made the first measurements of polymer surface diffusion in the key limit of dilute concentration and he identified the important class of physical problems where diffusion is anomalous yet Brownian. His laboratory became interested in many instances of molecular mobility measured at the [[single-molecule]] level, including [[active matter]] and transport in [[living cells]].<ref name=":0" />

The other principal current area of Granick's research concerns Janus colloidal particles, their self-assembly at rest and driven outside [[wikt:equilibrium|equilibrium]]. The scientific importance is to understand [[natural selection]] in the colloid world.<ref name=":0" />

== Public service and international experience ==
{{Quote box
| quote = The goal of my lab’s research is to think like a molecule, to learn to second-guess what a molecule would decide to do when confronted by external constraints in its complex environment.
| source = Steve Granick<ref name=":0" />
| width = 250px
}}
Steve Granick served as Chair of the Department of Energy (DOE) Council on Materials Panel on Polymers at Interfaces and Chair of the Division of Polymer Physics of the American Physical Society (APS). He holds or has held honorary or visiting positions at numerous international universities.

==Honors and awards==
Granick was elected Member of the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]] in 2015,<ref name=":0" /> and Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/ |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> He is a Fellow of the American Physical Society. He is the recipient of numerous international awards, including the APS (American Physical Society) national Prize for Polymer Physics, the ACS (American Chemical Society) national Prize for Surface and Colloid Science, and the Paris-Sciences Medal.
